title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
Charging from zero
Starting from 0 V toward a supply \(V_s\):
\[
V(t) = V_s \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)
\]
Discharging back toward 0 V from \(V_s\) follows the mirror image, \(V(t) = V_s e^{-t/\tau}\).

title: Ohm’s law and power
text: The relationship every other circuit identity gets built on top of.

title: Ohm’s law and power
text:
The law
For a resistor, voltage and current are proportional:
\[
V = IR
\]
Power dissipated follows from \(P = VI\), substituted with Ohm’s law to give two more useful forms:
\[
P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
\]
The \(I^2R\) form is the one that matters for sizing: double the current through a fixed resistance and dissipation quadruples, not doubles — a common reason parts run hotter than expected after a “small” current increase.

text:

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Loaded divider
Once something draws current from the output node — an ADC input, another circuit — that load resistor \(R_L\) sits in parallel with \(R_2\), and the divider ratio changes:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2 \| R_L}{R_1 + (R_2 \| R_L)}, \qquad R_2 \| R_L = \frac{R_2 R_L}{R_2 + R_L}
\]
This is why a divider that measures correctly open-circuit can read low once connected to a real load — the rule of thumb is to keep \(R_L \gg R_2\), typically 10× or more.

title: About
text:
I’m a hardware engineer, and on any given day I might be reading about magnetics, debugging an IC datasheet, tuning a microcontroller peripheral, or writing the software that ties it all together. For a long time the notes from that ended up scattered across notebooks and apps on different devices, half-findable at best.
This site is where those notes live now — one place, organized by topic, with the math written out rather than just the result. Most pages carry a small calculator next to the derivation, so a formula isn’t just something to read but something to actually use on a real design.
It’s a running project: chapters get added as I work through new topics, and existing notes get revised as I learn more or find a cleaner way to derive something.

title: Buck-boost converter
text: The classic (inverting) buck-boost can step the output above or below the input, at the cost of an inverted polarity — the output is referenced negative to the input’s ground. Same ideal CCM treatment as the buck and boost pages.

title: Buck-boost converter
text:
Duty cycle
\[
\frac{|V_{out}|}{V_{in}} = \frac{D}{1-D} \quad \Rightarrow \quad D = \frac{|V_{out}|}{V_{in} + |V_{out}|}
\]
\(D < 0.5\) steps down, \(D > 0.5\) steps up — the same switch duty cycle range covers both directions, which is the whole appeal of the topology.

title: Buck-boost converter
text:
Inductor current
The inductor is charged from \(V_{in}\) only, during the on-time — same charging behavior as a boost:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw} L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]
And the output only sees current during the off-time, so — again like a boost —
\[
I_{L,avg} = \frac{I_{out}}{1-D}
\]
This is the least efficient of the three topologies in practice: the inductor carries both the input and output current duty cycles, so RMS current (and core/copper loss) tends to be the highest of the three for a given output power.

title: LC and RC filter design
text: The two filters you reach for constantly: a simple RC low-pass for signal-level filtering, and an LC low-pass for power-stage or EMI filtering where you can’t afford a resistor’s power loss.

title: LC and RC filter design
text:
RC low-pass
A single resistor and capacitor to ground give a first-order (−20 dB/decade) low-pass with cutoff:
\[
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}
\]
Simple, but the resistor dissipates power continuously — fine for a signal line, not for filtering a DC-DC converter’s output current.

Calculator

title: LC and RC filter design
text:
LC low-pass
Replacing the resistor with an inductor removes the continuous power loss — the standard choice at a converter’s output or as an input EMI filter. Second-order (−40 dB/decade) response:
\[
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}
\]
For a target cutoff, there’s a free parameter — usually chosen via the filter’s characteristic impedance \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}\), which should roughly match the source/load impedance to avoid ringing:
\[
L = \frac{Z_0}{2\pi f_c}, \qquad C = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c Z_0}
\]
A too-low \(Z_0\) makes for a large capacitor and a peaky, underdamped response without added series resistance; too high makes for a large, lossy inductor. Real designs also check the \(Q\) at \(f_c\) against the source/load resistance and add damping if it rings.

Calculator

title: Zener and Schottky diodes
text: Two diode variants built around a normal PN junction’s least-wanted properties — breakdown and switching delay — turned into features.

title: Zener and Schottky diodes
text:
Zener diodes
A standard diode’s reverse breakdown is destructive if the current isn’t limited — but a Zener is doped specifically to break down at a well-controlled voltage \(V_Z\) and survive it indefinitely, provided power dissipation stays within its rating. That gives a cheap, if imprecise (a few percent, and temperature-sensitive), voltage reference.

Basic shunt regulator
A series resistor from the supply into the Zener (with the load in parallel) sets the Zener current; the resistor must be sized so the Zener always sees at least its minimum regulation current, across the full load current range:
\[
R = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{I_Z + I_{load}}
\]
Simple and lossy — the series resistor burns power continuously, and regulation is only as good as the Zener’s own impedance. Fine for a low-current reference or bias supply, not for anything power-hungry (a linear or switching regulator does the same job far more efficiently).


Calculator

title: Zener and Schottky diodes
text:
Schottky diodes
A Schottky diode replaces the PN junction with a metal-semiconductor junction. Two practical consequences follow directly from that:
Lower forward voltage — typically 0.2–0.4 V versus 0.6–0.7 V for silicon PN — because there’s no minority-carrier injection barrier to overcome in the same way.
No reverse-recovery time — a PN diode stores minority charge while conducting and takes tens to hundreds of nanoseconds to stop conducting when reverse-biased; a Schottky is a majority-carrier device with essentially none of that, so it switches off almost instantly.
That combination is exactly why Schottkys show up as the freewheeling/catch diode in unsynchronized buck converters and as reverse-polarity protection where the forward drop matters. The trade-offs: higher reverse leakage current (worse with temperature) and generally lower reverse voltage ratings than comparable PN diodes.

title: Diodes
text:
A diode is a single junction between P-type material (doped with acceptor atoms, majority carriers are holes) and N-type material (doped with donor atoms, majority carriers are electrons). Where they meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving behind a region stripped of free carriers — the depletion region — with a built-in electric field opposing further diffusion.
Forward bias (P side positive relative to N) narrows the depletion region and, past a threshold, lets current flow easily. Reverse bias widens it and current stays near zero — until reverse breakdown.



Fig. 1 — diode symbol, and current vs. voltage for both bias directions.

title: Diodes
text:
A diode is a single junction between P-type material (doped with acceptor atoms, majority carriers are holes) and N-type material (doped with donor atoms, majority carriers are electrons). Where they meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving behind a region stripped of free carriers — the depletion region — with a built-in electric field opposing further diffusion.
Forward bias (P side positive relative to N) narrows the depletion region and, past a threshold, lets current flow easily. Reverse bias widens it and current stays near zero — until reverse breakdown.



Fig. 1 — diode symbol, and current vs. voltage for both bias directions.

title: Diodes
text:
The diode equation
\[
I = I_S \left( e^{V / (nV_T)} - 1 \right)
\]
\(I_S\) is the reverse saturation current (tiny, often pA–nA), \(n\) is the ideality factor (close to 1 for a good diode), and \(V_T = kT/q \approx 25.85\,\text{mV}\) at room temperature. The exponential is why forward voltage looks almost like a fixed ~0.6–0.7 V (silicon) rather than a smooth ramp — current changes by roughly 10× for every ~60 mV of forward voltage.
Forward voltage drops slightly with temperature, about \(-2\,\text{mV/°C}\) for silicon — worth remembering when a design runs hot.

title: Diodes
text:
Rectification
A single diode passes only one half of an AC waveform (half-wave rectification). Four diodes in a bridge pass both halves in the same direction (full-wave), roughly doubling the ripple frequency seen by the output filter capacitor and halving the required capacitance for the same ripple — the same \(C = \Delta I / (f \cdot \Delta V)\) relationship as the buck converter’s output cap, just driven by load current instead of inductor ripple current.

title: Diodes
section: Calculator: series resistor for a diode or LED
text:
Calculator: series resistor for a diode or LED
The most common practical use of the diode equation: given a supply and a target forward current, size the series resistor. Treats the diode’s forward drop as roughly constant, which is accurate enough for design work once \(V_f\) is known from a datasheet.
\[
R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_f}{I_f}
\]

title: MOSFETs
text: A voltage on an insulated gate creates (or removes) a conductive channel between source and drain — no gate current flows in steady state, which is the main practical difference from a BJT’s current-controlled base.

title: MOSFETs
section: Enhancement vs. depletion, N vs. P channel
text:
Enhancement vs. depletion, N vs. P channel
Enhancement-mode devices (the vast majority in use today) are off at \(V_{GS}=0\) and need gate voltage past a threshold to turn on — safer as a default state, which is why they dominate. Depletion-mode devices are on at \(V_{GS}=0\) and need gate voltage to turn off. N-channel conducts with electrons and needs positive \(V_{GS}\); P-channel conducts with holes and needs negative \(V_{GS}\). N-channel is preferred where possible — electron mobility gives lower on-resistance for the same die area.

title: MOSFETs
text:
Regions of operation
Let \(V_{ov} = V_{GS} - V_{th}\) (the “overdrive” voltage). Using the simple square-law model:

Cutoff: \(V_{GS} < V_{th}\), no channel, \(I_D = 0\).
Triode / linear: \(V_{DS} < V_{ov}\), behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor: \(I_D = k\left(V_{ov}V_{DS} - \frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right)\)
Saturation: \(V_{DS} \geq V_{ov}\), current roughly flat (ideally independent of \(V_{DS}\)): \(I_D \approx \frac{k}{2}V_{ov}^2\)

Power MOSFETs are almost always operated either fully in triode (as a low-resistance switch) or fully off — the region in between is where switching loss happens, and a well-designed switching circuit spends as little time there as possible.

title: MOSFETs
text:
On-resistance and conduction loss
For a MOSFET used as a switch, the datasheet parameter that matters most is \(R_{DS(on)}\) — resistance while fully on. Conduction power loss follows directly:
\[
P_{cond} = I_{RMS}^2 \cdot R_{DS(on)}
\]
\(R_{DS(on)}\) rises with temperature (typically 30–50% higher at 125°C than at 25°C) and with gate drive that’s lower than the datasheet test condition — both worth checking against the datasheet curves, not just the headline number.

title: MOSFETs
text:
Calculator: conduction loss



Switching loss — the energy lost transitioning through the linear region on every turn-on/turn-off — depends on gate charge \(Q_g\), drive strength, and switching frequency, and generally dominates conduction loss at higher frequencies. Worth its own page once it’s next in the queue.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text: Two back-to-back PN junctions sharing a thin middle layer. A small current into the base controls a much larger current between collector and emitter — the mechanism behind both analog amplification and simple switching.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
NPN vs. PNP
NPN: emitter and collector are N-type, base is a thin P-type layer; current flows collector-to-emitter, conventional base current flows in. PNP is the mirror image — emitter/collector P-type, base N-type, currents reversed. NPN is more common in modern designs since electrons (the majority carrier doing the work in an NPN) have higher mobility than holes, giving better high-frequency performance for a given geometry.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
Current relationships
\[
I_C = \beta I_B, \qquad I_E = I_C + I_B
\]
\(\beta\) (also written \(h_{FE}\)) is typically 100–300 for small-signal parts, but varies significantly with temperature, collector current, and from device to device even within the same part number — never design something that depends on a precise \(\beta\) value.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
Operating regions

Cutoff: \(V_{BE}\) below ~0.6 V, no base current, transistor is off.
Active: base-emitter junction forward biased, base-collector junction reverse biased. \(I_C \approx \beta I_B\), roughly independent of \(V_{CE}\) (the slight upward slope in the figure is the Early effect). This is the amplifier region.
Saturation: both junctions forward biased, \(V_{CE}\) drops to a small value (~0.1–0.3 V), \(I_C\) is limited by the external circuit rather than \(\beta I_B\). This is the “fully on” switch region.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
Calculator: voltage-divider bias point
The standard way to bias an NPN in the active region: a resistor divider sets a stable base voltage, an emitter resistor stabilizes the operating point against \(\beta\) variation.
\[
V_B = V_{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}, \qquad I_E \approx \frac{V_B - 0.7}{R_E}, \qquad V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C(R_C+R_E)
\]



If \(V_{CE}\) comes out near 0 or negative, the resistor values are driving the transistor into saturation rather than the active region — reduce \(R_C\)/\(R_E\) or the base voltage.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
As a switch
Used as a switch, the goal is deliberately deep saturation rather than a well-controlled active-region current. Choosing enough base current to guarantee saturation across the worst-case (minimum) \(\beta\), with margin — a “forced \(\beta\)” of 10 rather than the datasheet’s typical 100–300 is a common conservative choice:
\[
I_{B} = \frac{I_{C}}{\beta_{forced}}, \qquad R_B = \frac{V_{in} - 0.7}{I_B}
\]

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text: A thyristor is a four-layer PNPN device that behaves like nothing else on this page: it latches. A gate pulse triggers it into conduction, and it then stays conducting — no continued gate drive needed — until the main current drops below a minimum holding current \(I_H\), at which point it turns off on its own.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text:
Silicon-controlled rectifier (SCR)
The basic thyristor: conducts in one direction only, like a diode, but stays off even when forward biased until the gate receives a trigger pulse. Once triggered and above \(I_H\), the gate loses all further control — the only way to turn it off is to bring the main current below \(I_H\), which in an AC circuit happens automatically every half-cycle as the waveform crosses zero.
That zero-crossing turn-off is exactly what makes SCRs useful for phase-controlled AC power delivery: triggering the gate at a chosen delay (firing angle \(\alpha\)) after each zero crossing controls how much of each half-cycle actually reaches the load, and the device turns itself off cleanly at the next crossing regardless.

Phase control and RMS output
For a resistive load, delaying the firing angle \(\alpha\) (0 to \(\pi\) radians within each half-cycle) reduces the RMS voltage delivered to the load:
\[
V_{RMS} = V_{in,RMS}\sqrt{1 - \frac{\alpha}{\pi} + \frac{\sin(2\alpha)}{2\pi}}
\]
\(\alpha = 0\) delivers the full waveform; \(\alpha = \pi\) delivers none. This is the mechanism behind old-style incandescent light dimmers.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text:
TRIAC
An SCR only conducts one direction, so it only controls one half of an AC waveform. A TRIAC is functionally two SCRs wired anti-parallel in a single package, controllable from a single gate — it conducts (and can be triggered) on both half-cycles, which is why it’s the part actually found in most household dimmers and AC motor speed controls rather than a pair of discrete SCRs.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text:
A caution worth stating plainly
Thyristor circuits usually work directly with mains voltage. That combination of high voltage and latching behavior (a triggered device won’t turn off just because the gate signal goes away) is genuinely dangerous to prototype casually — isolation, proper fusing, and mains-rated components matter here more than almost anywhere else on this site.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text: A quick derivation of solenoid inductance from first principles, then the practical correction engineers actually use, with a calculator to try real turn counts and dimensions.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
The ideal case
Treating the coil as infinitely long, Ampere’s law gives a uniform field inside: \(B = \mu_0 n I\), where \(n = N / l\) is turns per unit length. Flux linkage through all \(N\) turns gives:
\[
L_{ideal} = \mu_0 N^2 \frac{\pi r^2}{l}
\]
This overestimates inductance for any real, finite coil — it ignores fringing at the ends.



Fig. 1 — field concentrated inside the winding, with fringing paths returning outside.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
Wheeler’s correction
For a real single-layer coil where length isn’t much greater than radius, Wheeler’s 1928 approximation is the standard practical formula (\(r\), \(l\) in inches, result in \(\mu H\)):
\[
L_{\mu H} \approx \frac{r^2 N^2}{9r + 10l}
\]
Valid roughly for \(l > 0.4r\). Below that, it undercorrects and a full Nagaoka-coefficient treatment is needed.



Fig. 2 — field strength rising with current, fringing appearing at the ends.

title: Buck converter
text: A buck converter steps a DC input down to a lower DC output by switching an inductor between the input and ground, then filtering the result. This is the ideal, continuous-conduction-mode (CCM) analysis — enough to pick a starting inductor and output capacitor.

title: Buck converter
text:
Duty cycle
Ignoring losses, the output is set entirely by duty cycle:
\[
D = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}
\]

title: Buck converter
text:
Inductor selection
While the switch is on, the inductor sees \((V_{in} - V_{out})\) across it for time \(D/f_{sw}\); while off, it sees \(-V_{out}\) for \((1-D)/f_{sw}\). Either way gives the same ripple current:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{out}(1 - D)}{f_{sw} L}
\]
Solving for \(L\) at a target ripple (commonly 20–40% of \(I_{out}\)):
\[
L = \frac{V_{out}(1-D)}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]

title: Buck converter
text:
Output capacitor
Assuming the ripple is dominated by capacitance (not ESR), the output voltage ripple is approximately:
\[
\Delta V_{out} \approx \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\, f_{sw}\, C_{out}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad C_{out} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\, f_{sw}\, \Delta V_{out}}
\]
Real capacitors also add ESR-driven ripple (\(\Delta V_{ESR} = \Delta I_L \cdot R_{ESR}\)) on top of this — worth checking separately against the datasheet ESR once a part is chosen.

title: Boost converter
text: A boost converter steps a DC input up to a higher DC output by storing energy in an inductor while a switch is closed, then dumping it into the output (through a diode or synchronous switch) once it opens. Ideal CCM analysis again.

title: Boost converter
text:
Duty cycle
\[
D = 1 - \frac{V_{in}}{V_{out}}
\]

title: Boost converter
text:
Inductor current
While the switch is on, the full input voltage sits across the inductor, so ripple current is:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw} L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]
Unlike a buck, the inductor carries the input current, not the output current — this is why boost converters need bulkier inductors for the same output power. By power balance (\(V_{in}I_{in} = V_{out}I_{out}\), ideal):
\[
I_{L,avg} = I_{in} = \frac{I_{out}}{1-D}
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Parallel
Resistors in parallel share the same voltage, and their currents add, giving a reciprocal sum:
\[
\frac{1}{R_{parallel}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}
\]
The parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor — adding a path for current can only make it easier for current to flow.

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
Series RLC magnitude
For R, L, and C in series, the reactances subtract (they’re 180° apart) before combining with resistance:
\[
|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}
\]
This hits a minimum, \(|Z| = R\), at the resonant frequency where \(X_L = X_C\).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text: Calculator
